title: Talks
text:
‘Short-circuit’ talks, part 1

NEMX.jl: an open-source Julia package for NEM dispatch modelling
Dr Ghulam Mohy Ud Din
CSIRO
NEMX.jl is a Julia package for simulating dispatch in the Australian
National Electricity Market. It provides three complementary dispatch
models: (1) a zonal model that runs directly on the NEMDE/NEMWEB
database and reproduces historical dispatch prices; (2) a nodal model
built on the physical Synthetic NEM Network, also driven by NEMWEB data,
which reproduces dispatch prices under a range of network formulations
from DC through convex relaxations to non-convex AC representations; and
(3) lightweight OPF/FCAS models designed for long-term, market-informed
planning studies.
The session will give an overview of the package and its
capabilities, present benchmark simulations against historical NEM
outcomes, and walk through how to set up and run the tool. It will close
with a live demonstration of a BESS dispatch investigative study,
showing how NEMX.jl can be used to analyze storage behavior and its
impact on market outcomes.
Repository: github.com/csiro/ensys-NEMX.jlDocumentation and BESS study: csiro.github.io/ensys-NEMX.jl/dev/bess_study


OpenISP: an open-source electricity system model based on AEMO’s
Integrated System Plan
Ellie Kallmier, Dylan McConnell, Nicholas Gorman
The University of New South Wales
The OpenISP project is building an open-source, accessible and
transparent electricity system model based on the Australian Energy
Market Operator’s (AEMO) Integrated System Plan (ISP) methodology and
data. This initiative aims to facilitate wider access to energy system
modelling and enable more rapid, inclusive collaboration across
researchers, policymakers, and institutions. This presentation will
provide an introduction to the OpenISP modelling suite, alongside a
showcase and opportunities for discussion and feedback from the broader
energy research community.
Open-ISP project: github.com/Open-ISP


Resource adequacy modelling suite for the NEM
Tim Kopka, Muhammad Yasirroni, Pablo Apablaza, Bastian Moya, Sleiman Mhanna, Pierluigi Mancarella
The University of Melbourne
With the projected retirement of thermal coal power plants and the
associated increase in the penetration of variable renewable energy
sources and storage in the National Electricity Market (NEM), ensuring
reliability across all timesteps will depend strongly on the operation
of storage units. In adequacy assessments, storage behaviour is often
simplified, adopting, for example, perfect foresight of outage
conditions or heuristic, adequacy-optimistic operational approximations.
However, operational experience increasingly challenges these
assumptions, highlighting a discrepancy between modelled and real-world
storage behaviour and leaving the implications of these approximations
for NEM adequacy uncertain. To support reliability planning in the NEM,
we present an open-source adequacy assessment methodology and related
tools developed as part of the Australian Research in Power Systems
Transition (AR-PST) Stage 5. We evaluate adequacy under AEMO’s 2024
Integrated System Plan assumptions, comparing different operational
representations and their implications for reliability. Results show
that reliability levels of the NEM become sensitive to storage operation
approximations post-2030, and assumptions about state of charge,
charging behaviour, and dispatch incentives materially change the
estimated reliability risk.
Modelling suite: github.com/ARPST-UniMelbReport (AR-PST Stage 5, Topic 4-1): www.csiro.au/en/research/technology-space/energy/Electricity-transition/AR-PST/Stage-5


Energy Research Information Stack (ERIS)
Dr Michael Thomas
The Australian National University
We are seeing research projects emerge that combine two or more
actively developed open-source energy modelling tools in fun and
interesting ways. However, combining these tools on an ad-hoc and manual
basis is not only time consuming, but minimises understandability,
robustness and reusability. ACES has developed an ecosystem of software
packages, called the Energy Research Information Stack (ERIS), to
improve the interoperability of existing and emerging open-source
modelling software.
ERIS: bsgip.github.io/eris


Model-Based Systems Engineering for Alumina Decarbonisation
Adnan Qamar
CSIRO
As part of Work Package 4 of the HILT CRC, NEAC is applying a
Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) framework, integrated with
Hetero-Functional Graph Theory (HFGT), to support decarbonisation
planning for Australian heavy industry. The current case study focuses
on the Worsley alumina refinery, where a formally verified systems model
has been developed to represent the Bayer process, including digestion,
evaporation, precipitation, calcination, and associated steam and water
networks.
Rather than constructing standalone demand or supply models, the
framework provides an integrated representation of industrial processes
and multi-carrier energy systems within a single optimisation
environment. This enables the evaluation of technology substitution
pathways, electrification strategies, and carbon-price scenarios while
preserving system-level operational constraints.
The approach supports identification of least-cost decarbonisation
pathways, quantification of fuel-switching thresholds, and assessment of
infrastructure requirements under alternative transition scenarios. The
presentation will demonstrate how systems engineering methods can
enhance transparency, reproducibility, and cross-sector integration in
industrial decarbonisation studies, and will discuss opportunities for
open and interoperable modelling tools within the broader energy
modelling community.


How open is your modelling?
Wendy Russell1, Dora He1, Ehsan Nabavi1, Sophie Adams2
1The Australian National University 2La Trobe University
We have been working on how to open up energy modelling to social
insights and participatory processes. Much modelling deals with social
dimensions of the energy system (e.g. consumer actions and practices;
decisions of individuals and organisations; equity and the distribution
of costs, benefits and risks), but often through assumptions that are
not always supported with social evidence, nor transparent to the users
of modelling outputs. In addition, while modelling can underpin
operational, investment and policy decisions with wide-reaching social
implications, it often excludes input and engagement by non-experts and
the publics it is intended to ultimately benefit.
Our research considers ways to integrate social insights into
modelling, using both quantitative and qualitative approaches, and how
to use models to engage with different stakeholders and publics. We are
looking at iterative ways that use models to communicate about systems
with non-experts, and to use non-expert input to refine models. We will
briefly discuss our progress and approaches, and invite workshop
participants to discuss with us how their models could be used to open
up to non-expert participation.

title: Talks
text:
‘Short-circuit’ talks, part 2

Modelling green industrial hubs in Indonesia
Dr Jenny Haywood
CSIRO
The Government of Indonesia (GoI) is interested in developing new
industrial hubs that support the use of local capabilities, including
workforce and skills, renewable energy resources, land and
infrastructure. CSIRO has developed an online modelling tool to support
the GoI in decision-making on the supply of energy infrastructure to
meet the demand of new industrial hubs. The model optimises for
least-cost supply of energy (electricity and hydrogen), within
constraints such as land, renewable energy resources, transmission and
government policy. The tool will be demonstrated during the
presentation, for a case study site in Indonesia, Batam Island.


AEMC market modelling toolkit - an extended weather reference year
dataset
Daniel Condon
Australian Energy Market Commission
This talk will cover a new open-source dataset, developed by the AEMC
and hosted by the CSIRO, which encompasses projected renewable output
and demand across the National Electricity Market (NEM) based on 85
years of historical weather data, from 1945 to 2025. This dataset was
developed using machine learning techniques on historical reanalysis
weather data and AEMO’s operational market data, and is aimed at helping
researchers, modellers and policy-makers understand the impact of
weather on dispatch outcomes and reliability in the NEM.


Modelling investment uncertainty: agent-based modelling to quantify
economic uncertainty
Markus Mannheim
Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
Modelling investment uncertainty: agent-based modelling to quantify
economic uncertainty for different parties, to inform government
decision making.
More to come.


Power-system experiments in the browser: Tellegen and PowerIO
Prof Fred Geth
The University of Queensland
What if exploring a power-system model started with opening a web
page? This talk introduces Tellegen and PowerIO, open-source tools for
interactive power-system studies in the browser. PowerIO reads and
converts network data, while Tellegen provides power-flow and
optimal-power-flow calculations and visualisation. A short demonstration
will show how changing demand or a line rating produces an immediate
sensitivity-based preview, followed by a fresh solve. Case files and
calculations remain on the user’s device. The talk will explore
opportunities for teaching, research and sharing executable studies,
with further demonstrations and hands-on discussion during the
open-floor session.

title: Talks
text:
Panel session

Trustworthy Computational Research in the Age of AI
A/Prof Archie Chapman
The University of Queensland
Generative AI is rapidly becoming embedded in software- and
data-intensive research, creating new opportunities alongside new
integrity risks. Drawing on the principles of the Australian Code for
the Responsible Conduct of Research, this talk will explore how
established practices including verification and validation,
benchmarking, open-source software development, data stewardship, and
transparent workflows provide a foundation for the responsible use of AI
in research. Using examples from energy systems modelling and
computational science, I will discuss practical issues such as
AI-assisted software development, management of sensitive data, public
versus private repositories, software and data licensing, and
reproducibility in increasingly automated research environments. The
central argument is that AI does not diminish the importance of research
integrity principles; rather, it makes rigorous computational research
practices more important than ever, while also creating new
opportunities for research translation and impact.


Interoperability in open-source energy modelling tools
Dr Michael Thomas
The Australian National University
.. to fully realise the potential of interoperable open-source
software, we suggest growing and supporting a strong and enthusiastic
energy modelling community. In this workshop we will discuss the steps
need to achieve interoperability in open-source energy modelling tools
and ask open questions on how we might go about growing and supporting
the Australian energy modelling community.
ERIS: bsgip.github.io/eris


Open-source modelling at CSIRO
Dr James Foster
CSIRO
The story of how we’ve evolved over time to using increasing
open-source modelling in our work and the various transition points
along the way that we chose based on the circumstances at the time.
More to come.


Building consensus and participation around shared energy models
Prof Fred Geth
The University of Queensland
Building shared energy models requires agreement on what the data and
equations mean, which assumptions are appropriate, and how those
decisions can evolve. Drawing on my experience with collaborative
distribution-system modelling, I will discuss how communities work
towards that agreement and encourage people to contribute. Topics
include making modelling choices explicit, turning disagreements into
reviewable proposals, and creating useful entry points through examples,
data, documentation and technical review. The discussion will consider
how to balance a coherent shared specification with different research
needs, and how to turn initial interest into sustained participation.
These questions offer practical starting points for strengthening
collaboration across the Australian open-source energy modelling
community.
